title: Stony Brook University
summary: Stony Brook University stands on the territory the university identifies as Wopowog, connected to the Setalcott people. Its campus relationships include Algonquian language revitalization, an Indigenous language and art exhibition, Native American and Indigenous Studies, and support for Native students.
map_geometry_source: Official Stony Brook University address and maps/directions page; point is an approximate campus-level geocode and does not identify a sensitive cultural location.
why_this_matters: Stony Brook is a living Long Island example of Indigenous language revitalization, Native-led and Native-connected scholarship, public art, and student support taking place on Setalcott territory.
history_title: Indigenous language, scholarship, and community connections at Stony Brook
history_content:
Stony Brook University’s main campus is located in the place the university identifies as Wopowog, on the territory of the Setalcott people. That acknowledgment places the university’s contemporary work in Native American and Indigenous Studies within the living history of eastern Long Island, rather than treating Indigenous presence as only a subject of the past.

Language revitalization and the Algonquian library

The Department of Linguistics’ Algonquian Language Revitalization Project works with leaders from the Montaukett, Shinnecock, and Unkechaug Nations to support the revitalization of Eastern Long Island Algonquian languages. The project hosts courses in which Native community members and Stony Brook students learn together, and it maintains a library of materials on East Coast Native American languages and cultures. The university says the library, opened in 2023 in the Social and Behavioral Sciences Building, contains more than 1,500 items and has a public catalog.

Weaving Words, Weaving Worlds

The Paul W. Zuccaire Gallery’s 2025 exhibition Weaving Words, Weaving Worlds: The Power of Indigenous Language in Contemporary Art connected contemporary Indigenous art with language reclamation, cultural continuity, memory, and healing. Curated by Shinnecock artist Jeremy Dennis, the exhibition centered artists engaging with Algonquian languages spoken across Long Island and the Northeast, and included archival materials from Stony Brook Libraries’ Special Collections, including a Native Long Island map with more than 400 Algonquian words and cultural references.

Native American and Indigenous Studies

Beginning in spring 2025, Stony Brook’s interdisciplinary Native American and Indigenous Studies initiative offered a minor described by the university as the first of its kind on Long Island and the only such program at a public university in the region. The 21-credit minor includes core study in Indigenous history, literature, art, politics, environmental justice, and related fields; Algonquian language courses can count toward it. Its development included a steering committee with community leaders from the Montaukett, Shinnecock, Unkechaug, Setalcott, and Matinecock Nations.

The initiative’s founding director is Joseph M. Pierce, a citizen of Cherokee Nation. The university’s current faculty page identifies core faculty including Sicangu Lakota writer and English professor David Heska Wanbli Weiden, Karuk anthropologist Darcey Evans, Valeria Meiller, Shinnecock artist Courtney M. Leonard, and Vick Quezada, alongside affiliated faculty such as Andrew Newman, Paul Kelton, and Sebastián López-Vergara. Leonard joined the faculty in fall 2025, bringing an explicitly Shinnecock, water-centered artistic practice into the Art and NAIS programs. The initiative also connects scholarship with experiential learning and possible internships involving local community organizations, businesses, and tribal governments.

Support for Native students and community relationships

Stony Brook’s Native American Peoples Scholarship document describes a four-year scholarship intended to support qualified students from historically underrepresented Native American communities, with the Shinnecock and Unkechaug Nations specifically named in the program description. Students should contact Stony Brook’s Financial Aid office. The university has also documented Native American Heritage Month programming with Shinnecock, Unkechaug, and Matinecock elders and leaders, and a Native American Student Organization on campus.

These connections make Stony Brook a contemporary academic and cultural site: a university on Setalcott territory where local Native nations, language teachers, artists, students, scholars, and community partners have helped shape teaching, research, public exhibitions, and student support.
